questions.question: PDA TR13 was first issued in 1990. Which revision is the 2022 edition, and in which years was it previously revised?

options.A: The second revision, previously revised only once, in 2001
options.B: The third revision, previously revised in 2001 and 2014
options.C: The third revision, previously revised in 2004 and 2014
options.D: The fourth revision, previously revised in 1996, 2001 and 2014

questions.explanation: TR13 was first issued in 1990 and had been revised twice before (2001 and 2014); the 2022 edition is the third revision, intended to align with current industry trends and regulatory expectations.

questions.question: According to TR13, what is the role of the environmental monitoring (EM) program in sterile product manufacturing?

options.A: It replaces finished product sterility testing and becomes the only basis for batch release, with no need for other quality controls
options.B: It is used only to trace the source of contamination after a deviation occurs, is not part of the CCS, and is not used for routine trend monitoring
options.C: It specifically evaluates the mechanical performance and energy consumption of the facility HVAC, unrelated to contamination risks from process, personnel and utilities, and does not affect product quality
options.D: It confirms that the controls designed for contamination risks from the process, personnel, equipment, utilities and facility are correctly designed and continue to be effective, and is part of the CCS

questions.explanation: EM is used to confirm that the various contamination controls are correctly designed and continue to be effective, and it is an important part of the contamination control strategy (CCS). It cannot replace other controls and is not just a tool for after-the-fact tracing.

questions.question: The 2022 revision placed extra emphasis on several areas. Which of the following is NOT among them?

options.A: Validation details of finished product sterility test methods
options.B: Using quality risk management (QRM) principles to establish an EM program in practical steps
options.C: Higher expectations for data management and data integrity
options.D: Prerequisites for an effective EM program

questions.explanation: The focus of the new edition is QRM, data integrity, prerequisites, validation and maintenance of the qualified state of controlled environments, and rapid microbial methods (RMM) or automated monitoring systems. Validation of sterility test methods is not among them.

questions.question: A QA head is looking for guidance on "bioburden monitoring of drug substance intermediates and bulk products". Where does the TR13 scope statement suggest he look?

options.A: The risk assessment method in TR13 Section 5.2, setting bioburden alert levels for intermediates by following its steps
options.B: TR13 Section 6.1 on monitoring of terminal sterilization, using the bioburden trend table in it as the decision criterion
options.C: PDA TR69 (Bioburden and Biofilm Management)
options.D: TR13 Section 6.8, because that section covers microbial monitoring of all in-process intermediates and bulk

questions.explanation: Bioburden monitoring of bulk and intermediate products (other than pharmaceutical water) is not part of every EM program and falls outside the scope of TR13; see TR69 instead. Section 6.8 covers only pharmaceutical water.

questions.question: Which statement about the nature of the TR13 document is correct?

options.A: It has regulatory force and can replace the relevant FDA and EU requirements; a company that follows it is compliant
options.B: It is a technical guide that does not replace current or future regulations, and the latest regulations should still be consulted when implementing it
options.C: It applies only to the US market and does not address international practices such as those of the EU and PIC/S
options.D: It is a complete document covering all microbial control topics, with no need for other references or guidance

questions.explanation: TR13 states clearly that it should be regarded as technical guidance, is not intended to replace current or future regulations, and is not an all-encompassing document. Working group members come from global companies, and the content takes into account both US and international practices.

questions.question: Sampling results in an aseptic area exceed the alert level but have not yet exceeded the action limit. According to the TR13 glossary definitions, what is the most appropriate understanding?

options.A: Treat it immediately as the process being out of control, start a formal deviation investigation and suspend production in the area until results recover
options.B: It is still within the normal range and needs no follow-up; it is simply recorded at the next periodic review
options.C: It is an early warning of a departure from the normal state; it does not necessarily require corrective action, but review and follow-up should be strengthened
options.D: It means the cleanroom must undergo full revalidation, with all sampling locations and frequencies reassessed

questions.explanation: An alert level is an early warning, not necessarily grounds for corrective action, but it should trigger appropriate review and follow-up. Only exceeding the action limit indicates that the process has gone outside the normal operating range and requires a documented investigation and corrective action.

questions.question: Which of the following matches the TR13 definition of the "At Rest" state?

options.A: Equipment is installed and on standby with no personnel present (equivalent to static)
options.B: Normal equipment is operating, the specified number of personnel are present, and the process or a simulated process is in progress
options.C: The facility is built but equipment has not yet been installed (as built)
options.D: Personnel are present but all equipment is shut down and the process has not yet started

questions.explanation: At rest means no normal operations, with equipment installed and on standby and no personnel present, equivalent to static. The option about normal equipment operating with the specified number of personnel present describes In Operation (equivalent to dynamic).

questions.question: According to the TR13 glossary, what is the difference between Open RABS and Closed RABS?

options.A: In Open RABS, air is exhausted inside the cabinet through return ducts; in Closed RABS, the barrier has vents to the surrounding Grade B area
options.B: Open RABS needs no gloves during the whole operation, with all manipulations done directly by hand; Closed RABS must use gloves
options.C: Open RABS can be opened at any time for manipulation; Closed RABS is completely sealed during operation, with no air exchange with the outside and no return air
options.D: Open RABS has vents in the barrier, with air flowing from the RABS to the surrounding area; in Closed RABS, air is exhausted inside the cabinet through return ducts

questions.explanation: The two differ in how air is exhausted: Open RABS has vents in the barrier that let air flow to the surrounding Grade B area; in Closed RABS the air is recirculated through return ducts inside the cabinet. The option stating that Open RABS air goes out through return ducts inside the cabinet reverses the two.

questions.question: Which statement about the TR13 glossary's distinction between microbial characterization and microbial identification is correct?

options.A: Characterization determines genus and species; identification describes organisms by morphology and Gram reaction without classification, and must be performed together with strain typing
options.B: Characterization describes a microorganism by morphology, Gram reaction and key diagnostic tests; identification determines the genus and, where possible, the species
options.C: The two have the same meaning; they differ only in the terminology used by different regulations such as FDA, EU and PIC/S
options.D: Identification places microorganisms into taxonomic groups according to similarity; characterization determines genus and species and may include strain typing

questions.explanation: Characterization is a description such as "Gram-positive, coagulase-negative cocci"; identification determines the genus and, where possible, the species. Placing organisms into taxonomic groups according to similarity and relatedness is classification.

questions.question: Which statement about spores and vegetative cells matches the TR13 glossary?

options.A: Bacterial spores are a highly stress-resistant dormant form; fungal spores are not highly resistant and are similar to vegetative organisms
options.B: Bacterial spores and fungal spores are equally highly resistant to environmental stresses such as desiccation, heat and disinfectants
options.C: A vegetative cell is a cell form in a dormant state that can tolerate most disinfectants
options.D: All microorganisms can form spores, so there are no microorganisms that exist only as vegetative cells

questions.explanation: The glossary states that bacterial spores are a highly resistant dormant form, whereas fungal spores are not; vegetative cells are the actively growing state, some microorganisms exist only as vegetative cells, and some spore-forming organisms can switch between the two states.

questions.question: Which of the following does ISO 14644-1 itself NOT specify, leaving it to individual regulatory authorities or standards bodies to decide?

options.A: Classification is based on the number of particles larger than a given size per cubic meter of air, which defines the classes
options.B: Classes run from ISO 1 to ISO 9, with a smaller number being cleaner and ISO 1 the strictest
options.C: ISO classes are based on the total number of airborne particles, without distinguishing viable from non-viable particles, and so reflect only particle concentration
options.D: Which of the as built, at rest or in operation states the area should be in

questions.explanation: ISO 14644-1 does not specify the operational state to be tested, nor the particle size thresholds to be used; these are decided by individual regulations or standards bodies, which is why the application of the ISO standard is "similar but slightly different" among them.

questions.question: According to the EU, PIC/S and WHO Grade A–D classification, which ISO classes does Grade B correspond to at rest and in operation, respectively?

options.A: ISO 5 at rest; ISO 5 in operation as well
options.B: ISO 5 at rest; ISO 7 in operation
options.C: ISO 7 at rest; ISO 8 in operation
options.D: ISO 7 at rest; ISO 5 in operation

questions.explanation: Grade B is ISO 5 at rest and ISO 7 in operation. The option with ISO 5 in both states is Grade A (ISO 5 in both states), and the option with ISO 7 / ISO 8 is Grade C.

questions.question: What does TR13 give as the widely accepted guidance value of pressure differential (ΔP) between areas of different grades to ensure air flows from the cleaner area to the less clean area?

options.A: 2 to 5 Pa
options.B: 5 to 8 Pa
options.C: 10 to 15 Pa
options.D: 20 to 30 Pa

questions.explanation: The widely accepted guidance value is 10 to 15 Pa between areas of different grades. This differential is not needed for an open ISO 5 unidirectional flow area placed within an ISO 7 background.

questions.question: What are the action limits for airborne viable organisms (active air sampling) in EU Annex 1, PIC/S and WHO for Grade A, B, C and D, respectively?

options.A: <1, 10, 100, 200 CFU/m³ (by active sampling)
options.B: <1, 5, 50, 100 CFU/m³ (by active sampling, with continuous particle monitoring additionally required)
options.C: <1, 10, 50, 100 CFU/m³ (by active sampling)
options.D: <1, 5, 25, 50 CFU/m³ (by active sampling, applicable only to ISO 7)

questions.explanation: For active air the limits are <1 / 10 / 100 / 200 CFU/m³. The values <1, 5, 50, 100 are those for a 90 mm settle plate (per plate), and <1, 5, 25, 50 are the surface sampling limits for contact plates or swabs; both are easily confused with the air limits.

questions.question: Compared with other guidance, what is distinctive about how USP <1116> expresses microbial limits?

options.A: It uses CFU/m³ as the action limit, requiring less than 1 CFU/m³ for Grade A, with further gradations for the other grades
options.B: It requires all grades to monitor particles ≥0.5 µm and ≥5.0 µm at the same time, and uses particle counts in place of CFU limits, consistent with Annex 1
options.C: It follows the EU Grade A–D classification and its CFU excursion limits, taking the Annex 1 values as the reference
options.D: It replaces CFU excursion limits with the contamination recovery rate (CRR, the percentage of samples with microbial contamination), for example less than 1% for ISO 5

questions.explanation: USP <1116> uses the contamination recovery rate rather than CFU-count excursion limits: less than 0.1% for isolators or closed RABS, less than 1% for ISO 5, less than 5% for ISO 7 and less than 10% for ISO 8. Other guidance still uses CFU limits.

questions.question: According to TR13, what does cleanroom performance qualification (PQ) usually consist of?

options.A: Three consecutive runs under routine (in-operation) conditions
options.B: A single at-rest run
options.C: Two aseptic process simulations plus one at-rest measurement
options.D: Two consecutive in-operation runs under maximum personnel conditions are sufficient

questions.explanation: PQ usually consists of three consecutive runs under routine (in-operation) conditions. On the other hand, one run each for at-rest and in-operation total particle classification per ISO 14644-1 is considered sufficient, but that belongs to the OQ stage and is not a component of PQ.

questions.question: When performing at-rest viable sampling, which practice is consistent with TR13 for minimizing the influence of personnel?

options.A: Production operators take the samples, because they are most familiar with the room and equipment and know best which locations are prone to contamination
options.B: Surface sampling is done after the end of the run, to cover all activities, while measuring personnel activity at the same time
options.C: Surface sampling is done at the start of the run with only EM technicians present, and automatic samplers are set with a delay timer so that technicians can leave first
options.D: Maintenance personnel stay in the room during sampling to deal with equipment problems at any time and help change the plates, to ensure the equipment can always operate normally

questions.explanation: The purpose of at rest is to see the microbial control state of the room itself, so the influence of personnel should be excluded as much as possible: surface sampling is performed at the start of the run with only EM technicians present, and automatic samplers use a delay timer.

questions.question: After the initial PQ, why might an extended PQ also be performed?

options.A: To replace the initial PQ, shortening the overall validation timeline and eliminating all later routine requalification and sampling
options.B: To cover conditions the initial PQ may not have covered, such as seasonal microbial variation, establishment of alert levels and selection of disinfectant test strains
options.C: Specifically for HEPA filter leak testing and room classification, completed by the equipment vendor before shipment
options.D: Needed only after an aseptic process deviation occurs, with QA deciding at closure of the deviation whether to perform it

questions.explanation: An extended PQ is conducted over a period according to the routine sampling plan or extended sampling, to supplement conditions the initial PQ did not cover, such as seasonal variation, establishment of alert levels, selection of disinfectant test strains and further evaluation of the routine cleaning program.

questions.question: Before carrying out an EM risk assessment, what preparation does TR13 require?

options.A: Only the risk tool and software need to be chosen first; scope, objectives and ranking criteria can be set as the work proceeds, with documentation added later
options.B: It is completed by QC alone to keep the microbiology expertise consistent, with no other departments involved and no facilitator assigned, to avoid delaying the risk assessment
options.C: The goal is to maximize the number of sampling locations, with the risk question, ranking criteria and other matters added afterwards
options.D: First define the scope and objectives, the risk question statement, the risk tool and the ranking criteria, and assign a risk facilitator and a cross-functional team

questions.explanation: Before carrying out the assessment, the scope and objectives, risk question, risk tool and ranking criteria must be defined, and a risk facilitator leads a cross-disciplinary team covering microbiology, contamination control, quality, engineering, facilities and utilities, QC, QA and manufacturing.

questions.question: A new aseptic facility has completed EM PQ, and the results show that some sampling locations can be reduced while other areas need more. According to the lifecycle approach, what should be done next?

options.A: Keep all the PQ sampling locations as the routine plan with no adjustment, to stay fully consistent with the validation stage and facilitate annual data comparison
options.B: Adjust sampling locations only at the annual review, keeping the original locations in the meantime regardless of the PQ results
options.C: Adjust (reduce or add) sampling locations according to the PQ results and then establish the routine plan; later significant changes need to be evaluated and may require revalidation
options.D: Cancel routine sampling and keep only batch-related sampling, replacing area monitoring with finished product sterility testing

questions.explanation: The lifecycle approach adjusts sampling locations after PQ according to the results and then establishes the routine (and, where applicable, batch-related) sampling plan; significant changes such as reconstruction, process changes or equipment relocation need to be evaluated, and affected areas may need to be revalidated.

questions.question: Which statement about the nature of alert levels and action limits is consistent with TR13?

options.A: They are product specifications; exceeding them means the batch is rejected, and it may not be released regardless of the investigation result and must be entirely destroyed
options.B: They do not define product attributes (such as sterility) but detect environmental drift early; an action limit excursion at a critical aseptic step requires an investigation to be completed before release
options.C: Only exceeding the action limit needs to be documented; alert levels need no review and need not be included in trend reports or annual review
options.D: Once set they may not be revised, to keep historical data comparable, even if the process or facility has undergone major changes

questions.explanation: These limits are not product specifications; their purpose is to detect environmental drift before product quality is affected. Alert levels should be reviewed periodically and may be adjusted following improvements or changes; an action limit excursion at a critical aseptic step requires an investigation, including product impact assessment, to be completed before the affected batch is released.

questions.question: EM data are not normally distributed, and TR13 5.3.2 recommends using a nonparametric tolerance limit to set limits. To set an action limit at 95/99, what is the minimum amount of data required?
questions.explanation: 95/99 (action limit) requires at least N = 300; 95/95 (alert level) requires N = 60. EM data tend toward low or zero counts and are not normally distributed, so applying the mean plus 2 or 3 standard deviations directly is not appropriate.

questions.question: A site uses nearly 100 monitoring results to set an alert level and an action limit with the cutoff value approach. At which percentiles are the two set, respectively?

options.A: The 95th and 99th percentiles, respectively
options.B: The 99.9th and 99.99th percentiles, respectively
options.C: The 90th and 95th percentiles, respectively
options.D: The mean plus 1 and plus 2 standard deviations, respectively

questions.explanation: The cutoff value approach arranges the data in a histogram and sets limits at the values above which 5% and 1% of results lie, that is, the 95th and 99th percentiles. The option with the 99.9th and 99.99th percentiles is the nonparametric percentile method of 5.3.1.

questions.question: The contamination recovery rate (CRR) of an area is 1%. What does this mean?

options.A: 1% of CFU exceed the alert level
options.B: On average 1 CFU is recovered per square meter
options.C: Only 1% of samples show microbial contamination, regardless of the number of colonies
options.D: There are on average 0.01 colonies per plate

questions.explanation: CRR is the percentage of environmental samples with microbial contamination, independent of the number of colonies per sample. This also makes it applicable to emerging monitoring technologies whose signal is not CFU.

questions.question: After reading plates, an operator waits until the end of the shift and enters everything into the official form from memory. Which element of ALCOA does this most directly violate?

options.A: Attributable: data should identify who generated or recorded them, and when
options.B: Contemporaneous: data should be recorded at the time they are generated or observed
options.C: Legible: data should be readable and understandable, and remain readable throughout the retention period
options.D: Original: data should be the first recorded original record, or a verified true copy

questions.explanation: The "C" in ALCOA stands for contemporaneous: data are to be recorded at the moment they are generated or observed. TR13 also requires that raw data not be recorded on uncontrolled media such as informal forms or scrap paper.

questions.question: A site introduces an RMM for EM that measures a non-CFU signal, and its values cannot be directly mapped to the existing alert levels and action limits. What does TR13 recommend?

options.A: Accumulate enough data to set limits for the new method on a risk basis and correlate them with CFU where possible, or use trend analysis instead
options.B: Directly reuse the original CFU limits with no comparison or conversion, and revise them gradually as deviation cases accumulate
options.C: Because it cannot be mapped to CFU, RMM may not be used for EM, nor as a supplement or parallel method to traditional culture
options.D: As long as the equipment vendor provides the values, no further validation or limit setting is needed, and the vendor's recommended values can be adopted directly

questions.explanation: Users may revise limits based on historical data from the new method; the new limits need a reasonable basis and are finalized on a risk basis, and for Grade A, where zero counts are expected, trend analysis may be more suitable. The draft EU Annex 1 also requires that for results that differ from CFU, limits be scientifically justified and correlated with CFU where possible.

questions.question: In parallel comparison with traditional culture, why may RMMs that do not depend on microbial growth give higher values than the traditional method?

options.A: The culture media used by RMM are richer in nutrients, allowing more fastidious organisms to grow
options.B: RMM sampling volumes are always larger than with the traditional method, so the cumulative counts are higher
options.C: RMM always uses a longer incubation time, so slower-growing organisms are also counted
options.D: Traditional methods cannot detect VBNC, injured or dormant organisms, which an RMM may still detect

questions.explanation: RMMs that do not require growth can detect viable but not culturable, stressed or dormant organisms, so their values may be higher. This is also why it is hard to establish a direct correlation with CFU and why additional statistical analysis may be needed.

questions.question: According to the example identification scheme in TR13 Table 5.6-1, in which situation is strain typing or molecular fingerprinting needed?

options.A: Any microbial recovery in a Grade B area, regardless of species or number
options.B: A major product failure, such as a media fill failure, a sterility test failure or a significant adverse trend
options.C: An alert level excursion in a Grade D area, occurring two or more times in a row
options.D: As part of routine monitoring, periodic typing of all recovered colonies

questions.explanation: Strain typing is used in the case of major product failures. All recovered organisms from Grade A and B are identified to species (or genus if not possible), and for Grade C and D alert or action excursions and periodic identification in routine monitoring, identification to species or genus is also sufficient.

questions.question: Pseudomonas is recovered in a Grade C area. According to TR13, which source should be considered first?

options.A: Personnel skin, so gowning training and hand disinfection should be strengthened first
options.B: Soil, dust and air, so the building envelope should be checked first
options.C: Water sources; Gram-negative aquatic organisms may indicate water intrusion and need investigation
options.D: Equipment lubricants, so preventive maintenance and cleaning records should be reviewed first to rule out cross-contamination

questions.explanation: Pseudomonas is usually associated with water sources; aquatic Gram-negative organisms are an indicator of concern in an aseptic cleanroom and may indicate water intrusion and increase the risk of mold growth. Staphylococcus mostly comes from skin, and Bacillus and molds are mostly associated with soil, dust and air.

questions.question: A monitoring excursion occurs in a compressed gas system. According to TR13 Table 5.7-1, how should the investigation begin?

options.A: Only re-incubate the same sample to confirm whether it was an operator error, and take further action only if the result is the same
options.B: Directly review the personnel gowning procedure and training records, and strengthen gowning supervision and requalification
options.C: Review personnel activity and airflow patterns, and perform integrity testing and classification of the room-end HEPA
options.D: Immediately retest and perform a filter integrity test; if the retest confirms the excursion, replace the filter, and evaluate the impact on processed product

questions.explanation: The investigation elements for a compressed gas system are immediate retest, a filter integrity test, replacement of the filter once the retest confirms the excursion, and an evaluation of product impact. Personnel activity, airflow patterns and HEPA testing are investigation items for room air and HVAC.

questions.question: Comparing EM for terminal sterilization and aseptic processing, which statement is consistent with TR13?

options.A: For terminally sterilized products the most critical thing is airborne particle monitoring, which is more important than bioburden control
options.B: Terminal sterilization has far more sampling locations and a higher frequency than aseptic processing, and is controlled to Grade A standards
options.C: For terminal sterilization the most critical factor is the bioburden of the product and components to be sterilized; aseptic processing has clearly more sampling locations and a higher frequency
options.D: The depth and frequency of EM are the same for both, differing only in name, and the sampling plans can be fully shared

questions.explanation: Although environmental control still matters for terminal sterilization, the most critical factor is the bioburden of the product and components. EM for aseptic processing bears directly on sterility assurance, with clearly more sampling locations and a higher frequency, and EM data must be reviewed before batch release and excursion investigations closed.

questions.question: According to TR13, how does EM of an isolator differ from that of conventional aseptic filling?

options.A: Isolator gloves and half-suits are monitored at the end of each fill or campaign; the external air, surfaces and personnel need not be monitored after every fill
options.B: The isolator needs gloves and half-suits monitored only at annual requalification, and the rest, including the environment outside the isolator, needs no routine monitoring, trend analysis or investigation
options.C: Air, surfaces and personnel outside the isolator must be monitored after every fill, with the same number of sampling locations as conventional aseptic filling
options.D: Monitoring is needed only when a glove is found to be damaged, and only the damaged glove is monitored, while the environment outside the isolator is monitored after every fill

questions.explanation: EM of an isolator depends on its risks, especially the integrity of the half-suits and gloves. Gloves and half-suits are monitored at the end of each fill or campaign; contact surfaces inside the isolator that are sterilized or changed between batches are monitored before sterilization or replacement.

questions.question: What is the "Grade A air supply" mentioned in TR13?

options.A: An ISO 14644 cleanroom class with defined viable and particle limits, requiring continuous particle monitoring and to be used within a Grade B background
options.B: Used to protect stoppered but uncapped vials, with air passing through filters capable of Grade A particle quality, but the area itself is not classified and needs no continuous particle monitoring or Grade A viable limits
options.C: The type of air supply that must be used in all Grade B background areas, replacing terminal HEPA filters and pressure differential control, to be verified after every run and revalidated by the supplier every year
options.D: Replaces the continuous monitoring required in a Grade A area with an isolator, so that the whole filling line needs no particle or viable monitoring in any state

questions.explanation: The Grade A air supply introduced in Annex 1 is used for additional protection of stoppered vials before capping; it is not a cleanroom class, so it has no particle and viable limits. At least at validation and revalidation, testing is done at the point of air supply to confirm Grade A particle quality.

questions.question: Comparing active and passive sampling of viable air, which statement is correct?

options.A: Passive sampling can collect a large, homogeneous volume of air in a short time but may disturb airflow, so it should be included in airflow visualization studies
options.B: Active sampling can expose for up to 4 hours next to a critical process without affecting airflow, and can simulate the path of contamination reaching the critical process
options.C: Active sampling need not be included in airflow visualization studies, because the sampling head is small and does not disturb the airflow or unidirectional flow pattern
options.D: Active sampling can collect a large, homogeneous volume of air in a short time but may disturb airflow, so it should be included in airflow visualization studies; passive sampling can run for a long time without affecting airflow

questions.explanation: The characteristics of active and passive sampling are complementary, so the two can be used together to understand trends. The option describing passive sampling as collecting a large volume in a short time and disturbing airflow, and the option describing active sampling as exposing for up to 4 hours without affecting airflow, both swap the advantages and disadvantages of the two.

questions.question: Large-area sampling of the inner surface of a large tank or vessel is needed. Which surface monitoring method does TR13 recommend?

options.A: Surface rinse: rinse the inner surface with sterile diluent, collect it and test by membrane filtration, with the rinse holding time confirmed
options.B: Contact plate, rolled gently, with large inner surfaces rolled repeatedly to cover the whole area
options.C: A template of about 25 cm² with a swab, repeated many times to cover the whole surface, then combining the swabs for incubation
options.D: A flexible culture film applied over the whole inner surface, then removed in one piece and transferred to an incubator for incubation and counting

questions.explanation: Surface rinse is best for large-area sampling (such as kettles, equipment and tanks) and uses membrane filtration because of the large sample volume. Contact plates and flexible films suit flat surfaces, and swabs are suitable for equipment and irregular surfaces.

questions.question: TR13 Section 7.0 lists 16 EM prerequisites. Which three are considered basic pre-validation activities and are not elaborated further?

options.A: Audit and qualification of the culture media supplier, media release, confirmation of media shelf life and validation of shipping conditions
options.B: Sample holding studies and shipping, culture strategy and validation, EM equipment validation and calibration program
options.C: Selection of growth-promotion organisms, culture maintenance and storage, analyst training and qualification
options.D: IQ/OQ of HVAC/building automation system, HEPA filter certification, airflow pattern measurement

questions.explanation: Items 14 to 16 (IQ/OQ of HVAC/BAS, HEPA certification, airflow pattern measurement) are basic pre-validation activities, so they are not detailed further in that section. The other options are all items that are described in the section.

questions.question: For swab sampling in a Grade A environment, which culture medium does TR13 mention is usually used?

options.A: Always Sabouraud dextrose agar, whether or not bacteria need to be detected, with no other medium needed
options.B: Tryptic soy broth (qualitative result), although a suitable solid medium can be used instead for a quantitative result
options.C: Anaerobic medium for routine use, incubated and read entirely in an anaerobic chamber
options.D: Plain nutrient agar without neutralizers, to avoid neutralizers inhibiting microbial recovery

questions.explanation: Grade A swabs are usually placed in tryptic soy broth for a qualitative result, and a quantitative result can also be obtained from solid medium. Sabouraud is used only when fungal contamination of the facility is suspected, and anaerobic media are used depending on the risk situation.

questions.question: When selecting organisms for the growth promotion test (GPT) of culture media, what does TR13 require?

options.A: Use only the strains specified in the pharmacopoeia; environmental isolates need not be included, nor does their representativeness need to be evaluated, and growth performance need not be separately confirmed
options.B: Use only environmental strains isolated on site; pharmacopoeial strains need not be included, and their representativeness need not be evaluated
options.C: Include the strains required by the pharmacopoeia and representative environmental isolates, with the environmental organisms selected according to the microbial profile in routine trend reports
options.D: Choose any strains the laboratory has on hand, as long as they have an ATCC number, without considering representativeness

questions.explanation: GPT strains should cover both the strains required by the relevant pharmacopoeial chapters and representative environmental isolates. Using only pharmacopoeial strains is a common deficiency because it does not reflect the actual flora on site.

questions.question: What are the typical incubation conditions for EM samples described in TR13?

options.A: Total bacterial count 30 to 35 °C for 48 to 72 hours; total yeast and mold count 20 to 25 °C for 5 to 7 days
options.B: Total bacterial count 20 to 25 °C for 48 to 72 hours; total yeast and mold count 30 to 35 °C for 5 to 7 days
options.C: Both at 30 to 35 °C for 5 days
options.D: Bacteria 20 to 25 °C for 24 hours; yeast and mold 30 to 35 °C for 48 hours

questions.explanation: Bacteria are usually incubated at 30 to 35 °C for 48 to 72 hours, and yeasts and molds usually at 20 to 25 °C for 5 to 7 days. Industry surveys show that most companies use two-stage temperature incubation, starting with the lower temperature.

questions.question: Why does TR13 require a sample hold study?

options.A: To confirm that the culture medium is still effective within the shelf life stated by the supplier, and to decide the expiry for each lot
options.B: EM samples are sensitive to conditions such as sampling time and storage temperature, so handling between sampling and incubation needs to be validated
options.C: To determine the optimum incubation temperature for yeasts and molds, and to confirm the temperature uniformity and accuracy of the incubator
options.D: To verify the volume accuracy of the air sampler, and to confirm that the sampling flow rate and calibration certificate are within their validity

questions.explanation: Handling and storage conditions are considered critical parameters, so sample handling from the end of sampling to the start of incubation must be validated. Care is also needed when transferring media through a disinfection airlock with UV lamps.

questions.question: Which of the following is a check in cleanroom IQ rather than OQ?

options.A: Pressure differential measurement between adjacent rooms, and functional verification of the differential pressure alarms
options.B: Airflow visualization (smoke) studies, confirming the unidirectional flow pattern and airflow direction
options.C: Confirmation of the material and installation of the ductwork downstream of the terminal HEPA, and instrument calibration certificates
options.D: Room air classification (total particle counts), confirming that each sampling location meets the ISO 14644-1 class requirement

questions.explanation: IQ confirms that key system components meet user requirements and have been correctly identified, installed and calibrated, including the ductwork after the terminal filter and instrument calibration. Pressure differentials, smoke studies and room classification are all OQ tests.

questions.question: According to TR13 Appendix 1, under what conditions should cleanroom OQ be performed?

options.A: At rest: HVAC installed, commissioned and balanced, equipment installed and operating, no product or materials, and no personnel other than those necessary for testing
options.B: In operation: maximum personnel and worst-case activities at the same time, with filling operations performed with actual product
options.C: Only during an aseptic process simulation, completed at the same time as the media fill
options.D: As built, with equipment not yet installed, confirming only HVAC airflow, pressure differentials and room classification results

questions.explanation: OQ is performed at rest, with the equipment operating to verify the system's ability to control the particles generated by the equipment. In-operation conditions are used for EM PQ and physical parameter PQ.

questions.topic: OQ after a HEPA filter change
questions.question: The terminal HEPA filter (H14) in a Grade B room was replaced. According to TR13, which OQ tests are recommended?

options.A: Repeat all items in Table 9.3.2-1, including temperature, relative humidity and room pressure differential
options.B: Only temperature, relative humidity and room pressure differential; the other airflow and leak tests need not be repeated because of the filter change
options.C: Only air velocity, because it is the only necessary OQ test for a Grade B area
options.D: Airflow distribution, filter pressure drop, leak test and room classification; temperature, humidity and room pressure differential are not affected and need not be repeated

questions.explanation: Changing a filter does not affect temperature, humidity or room pressure differential, so only the air velocity (Grade A) or airflow distribution (Grades B, C, D), filter pressure drop, filter leak test (H13/H14 and above) and room classification are needed. The air velocity item for Grade B is N/A in the table.

questions.question: The initial frequency of routine requalification by HEPA leak testing for a Grade B room is every 6 months. After three consecutive successful tests, how does TR13 allow it to be adjusted?

options.A: Keep it at every 6 months; the frequency may not be adjusted on the basis of a successful record, and the regulatory authority must be notified
options.B: It may be extended to twice the initial frequency, that is, every 12 months
options.C: It may be extended to every two years, and the annual visual inspection is waived
options.D: The test may be waived entirely and replaced with monitoring of room pressure differentials

questions.explanation: After three consecutive successes, the frequency may be relaxed to twice the initial frequency: Grade B can move to annually and other grades to every two years. If a new filter is installed, at least three consecutive successes at the initial frequency must again be achieved.

questions.question: Routine requalification of room classification for a Grade A area is usually every 6 months, but under what circumstances may it be omitted?

options.A: For any Grade A area, because only other grades need routine requalification
options.B: Permanently, once three consecutive requalifications have been successful, with no classification testing needed afterwards
options.C: When continuous fixed particle monitoring is in place and that monitoring meets the requirements of ISO 14644-1
options.D: Only for Grade A areas inside isolators, whereas open Grade A areas must still be requalified every 6 months

questions.explanation: If a Grade A area has continuous fixed particle monitoring that satisfies ISO 14644-1, requalification of area classification is not needed. The three-success provision only relaxes the frequency; it is not a waiver.
